h1: Oil Tank Replacement Cost in New Brunswick: 2026 Guide
heroSub: Straight answers on what a new oil tank costs in Moncton and Southeast New Brunswick, and what removal runs on top. Free written estimates, no pressure. Call (506) 802-3471.
introHtml:
If you're pricing a new oil tank, you're probably holding an insurance letter or staring at rust streaks and wondering what this is going to cost. Here's the short version: most homeowners in Greater Moncton pay $3,000 to $5,500 for a new tank installed, plus $500 to $1,100 to remove the old one. Buried tanks and leak cleanups cost more, and we break all of it down below.

These are realistic 2026 numbers in Canadian dollars for Westmorland, Albert and Kent counties, not lowball teaser rates. Every job is a bit different, so treat this page as your starting point, then get a free written estimate for your exact setup. If your tank is actively leaking, skip the reading and call our 24/7 emergency line at (506) 802-3471.

sections.heading: What Changes the Price on Your Job
sections.html:
Two houses on the same street can get quotes hundreds of dollars apart, and it's usually not because somebody's getting ripped off. These are the factors that move the number the most:

  • Where the tank sits. An outdoor tank beside the house is the cheapest to swap. A basement tank has to be drained, cut down and carried up the stairs, which adds time and cost.
  • Tank material and size. A standard 910 litre steel tank is the budget option. Fibreglass costs more up front but can't rust from the inside out, so it tends to pay off over its life.
  • Access. Tight side yards, decks built over the tank, finished basements and deep winter snow all slow the crew down.
  • What's left in the old tank. Remaining oil has to be pumped out and either transferred to your new tank or disposed of properly, along with any sludge.
  • Lines, fittings and code upgrades. If your supply line, filter or fittings don't meet current code, they get replaced during the install and show up on the quote.
  • Timing. A planned swap in summer costs less than an emergency call during a February cold snap. Emergency work carries a $200 to $400 premium.

sections.heading: Removal Costs: Above Ground, Basement and Buried
sections.html:
Taking out an above-ground outdoor tank is straightforward work, which is why standard oil tank removal runs $500 to $900. Basement tanks run $700 to $1,100 because most went in before the house was finished, and they have to come out in pieces.

Buried tanks are the wild card. Buried oil tank removal starts around $2,000 and can reach $10,000 depending on depth, access and what shape the tank is in when it comes out of the ground. If the soil around it tests contaminated, remediation is a separate job that routinely runs into five figures, which is exactly why insurers push so hard to get old buried tanks out. Whichever removal you book, keep the disposal paperwork, since your insurer or a future buyer may ask for it.

sections.heading: Why Your Insurance Letter Changes the Math
sections.html:
Most oil tank replacements in New Brunswick don't start with a leak. They start with a letter saying your insurer won't renew unless the tank is replaced by a deadline. It can feel like a shakedown, but there's real logic behind it: a leaking tank can trigger cleanup costs in the tens of thousands, and standard policies often don't cover spills well.

Here's the practical takeaway. A planned tank replacement at $3,000 to $5,500 is a known, one-time cost, while a leak is an open-ended one. If your deadline is tight, tell us when you call and we'll work with it. Every estimate we give is free and in writing, so you'll have something solid to send your broker.

sections.heading: How to Get an Accurate Quote and Keep the Cost Down
sections.html:
Phone quotes are guesses. A real number comes from seeing your tank, your access and your oil lines, which is why we do free written estimates across Greater Moncton, Dieppe, Riverview and the surrounding communities out to Shediac and Sackville.

A few things that genuinely lower the bill: book in spring or fall instead of mid-winter, bundle removal and installation into one visit, and don't wait until your insurance deadline is a week away. When you compare quotes, make sure each one spells out the tank brand and material, whether removal and disposal of the old tank is included, whether new lines and a filter are included, and the total with tax. A quote that's $800 cheaper but leaves out removal isn't actually cheaper. We're licensed and insured, and the number we quote is the full, done price.

faq.q: How much does oil tank replacement cost in New Brunswick?
faq.a: Most homeowners pay $3,000 to $5,500 for a new tank installed, in 2026 Canadian dollars, with fibreglass tanks at the upper end of that range. Removing the old tank adds $500 to $1,100 for most above-ground and basement tanks. Always confirm in writing what the quote includes.

faq.q: Will my home insurance pay for a new oil tank?
faq.a: No, replacing an aging tank is treated as maintenance, the same as a new roof, so it comes out of your pocket. Insurers require it because leak cleanups are so expensive, and some policies limit or exclude oil spill coverage entirely, which is worth confirming with your broker.

faq.q: How much does it cost to remove a buried oil tank?
faq.a: Buried tank removal in Southeast New Brunswick typically runs $2,000 to $10,000 depending on depth, access and tank condition. If contaminated soil is found, remediation is a separate cost that often reaches five figures, so it pays to deal with a buried tank before it leaks.

faq.q: Is a fibreglass tank worth the extra money?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Fibreglass tanks can't rust from the inside out the way steel tanks do, they carry longer warranties, and many insurers treat them more favourably on age limits. If you plan to stay in your home for a while, the higher upfront cost often works out.

faq.q: What if my tank is leaking right now?
faq.a: Call our 24/7 emergency line at (506) 802-3471 right away, because a leaking tank is a soil problem, not just a heating problem. Emergency response adds $200 to $400 to the job, but acting fast is far cheaper than the five-figure remediation bill a spreading leak can cause.
